newsitem.title: CHINA: Chinese-Americans in HK told to apply for protecti.
newsitem.headline: Chinese-Americans in HK told to apply for protecti.

text.p: The U.S. government has advised Chinese-Americans in Hong Kong, now a special region of China, to register as foreign nationals if they want to be eligible for U.S. consular protection.

"Dual nationals who wish to ensure consular access and protection... must declare their U.S. nationality by presenting their U.S. passports and completing an application for declaration of change of nationality with the Hong Kong immigration department," the U.S. Consulate said in a notice.

The advisory said that if Americans of Chinese descent stayed for less than 30 days in Hong Kong they would get consular protection without having to declare their nationality should they get into trouble.
This provision applied to people of Chinese descent, born in either Hong Kong or China, under a Sino-U.S. agreement.
Under international law, consular protection does not apply to a dual nationality holder if he gets into trouble in one of his countries of citizenship.
Many Hong Kong Chinese people are both local permanent residents and foreign passport-holders. China does not recognise dual citizenship.

Hong Kong Chinese can either keep quite about their foreign citizenship and risk being treated as a Chinese national or declare themselves foreigners, losing their status as Chinese nationals while retaining Hong Kong residency rights as foreigners.
The U.S. Consulate-General estimates 40,000 Americans live in Hong Kong, where 156 years of British colonial rule ended on June 30.
